narration: CanLab reverse-engineers a CAN bus. This is a real recording from a CANedge logger: nine thousand six hundred frames across fifty arbitration identifiers, every one of them twenty-nine bit extended. Nothing here was simulated and nothing was labelled in advance.

The work is grouped into five workspaces rather than sixteen tabs in a row. Capture is what is on the wire, Explore is what it looks like over time, Detect is the automatic analysis, Define is where you write down what you worked out, and Bus is everything that talks back.
caption: Five workspaces, not sixteen tabs

narration: First question on an unknown bus: what is it. Twenty-nine bit identifiers usually mean a truck running J1939, but these carry data page one in the hundred and twenty-six thousand range, which is NMEA 2000. This is a boat. Vessel heading, rate of turn, wind, satellite positioning.
caption: Data page 1 in the 126k range: NMEA 2000, not J1939

narration: Which the decoded fields then confirm from three directions at once. Position puts the vessel at forty-two point six six north, eighty-one point two one west, on Lake Erie. Magnetic variation reads eight point nine degrees west, which is the published value for there. Speed over ground is exactly zero, so she was moored, and the wind was under a metre per second.
caption: Position, variation and speed agree with each other

narration: The frames table is a log, which is the wrong shape for the question you ask at the bench. The sniffer collapses the bus to one row per message: a byte turns green when it rises and red when it falls, and bytes that never move stay dim.
caption: One row per message, coloured by what just moved

narration: Notch is why this beats scrolling. It records every bit that is moving right now and ignores it from then on, so the counters that never stop go quiet and the next thing that lights up is the thing you did.
caption: Notch: ignore everything already moving

narration: One press masked four hundred and sixty four bits of steady traffic on this log.

The detectors run with no knowledge of the protocol at all. Here they find a counter in byte zero of twenty-three messages, wrapping at two hundred and fifty one. NMEA 2000 calls that byte the sequence identifier and specifies exactly that wrap. The detector got there from the data.
caption: Byte 0 counters, wrap 251, found without the spec

narration: Entropy per bit finds where one field ends and the next begins. Each candidate boundary carries a confidence, which is a match fraction over the frames loaded, not a proof.
caption: Field boundaries, ranked by confidence

narration: A signal is a message, a start bit, a length and a scale. The preview decodes real frames through the definition as you type, so it is checked against the bus rather than against your arithmetic. Nought point seven seven metres per second: light air, which is what a moored boat on a calm lake should read.
caption: Live decode of real frames, as you edit

narration: Drag across the grid to claim bits. Motorola byte order and non-contiguous layouts go through the same coordinate map the exporter uses, so what you select is what gets written out.
caption: Drag to claim bits; Motorola layouts included

narration: Plotted against time is where a definition is confirmed or refuted. Both traces are the same two bytes of the same message. The lower one reads them little-endian and wanders between nought point seven and nought point nine metres per second. The upper one reads them the other way round and claims the wind was blowing at two hundred. You do not need the spec to see which is right.

Everything that can put a frame on a wire is behind one gate. ARM TX is off by default and it covers injection, replay, fuzzing, gateway forwarding and every diagnostic request. Disarming stops a running worker within two seconds.
caption: Nothing transmits until this is armed

narration: Before any of that, the page shows the frame it would send. Byte one holds four D, which is seventy-seven hundredths of a metre per second, and the bytes the signal does not touch stay dim. If the vehicle profile writes a counter or a checksum, the bytes it overwrites turn amber.
caption: The eight bytes the controls above actually produce

narration: The controls themselves are three rows: which signal, what value, and how often. The slider spans whatever range the signal declares, and every send lands in the log underneath with its result.
caption: Pick a signal, set a value, send once or on a loop

narration: Three things can run alongside: a REST API, an MCP server that lets an assistant drive the analysis, and the plugin list. None of the twenty-five assistant tools can transmit; putting frames on a wire stays behind the gate where a person is watching.
caption: REST and MCP: read and analyse, never transmit

narration: Hardware is picked here. Every python-can backend is available, plus GVRET, which CanLab adds itself for the boards SavvyCAN runs on. Detect finds what is plugged in, and Test opens the adapter and listens for a second without transmitting.
caption: Any python-can backend, plus GVRET

narration: A second recording, and a different vehicle entirely: twenty-three minutes off a car, eleven bit identifiers, a hundred and fifty five thousand frames. One identifier carries a hundred and thirty three thousand of them. The sniffer folds the whole capture into sixteen rows in under a second.
Load a capture, work out what the bytes carry, write it down, and export a DBC other tools can read. Everything shown here ran against real recordings from hardware this project did not produce.
